query: How can melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties be determined accurately and efficiently across the high-entropy-alloy family? State the physical rationale, expected quantitative performance, range of applicability, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive validation result that would rule out the proposed approach.

generation.hypothesis: A combined high-throughput calorimetric-neutron imaging approach integrated with CALPHAD modeling can accurately and efficiently determine the melting temperature, fusion enthalpy and entropy, liquid-phase volume change at melting, and other thermodynamic properties across homogeneous high-entropy alloys.
generation.material_initial_state: High-entropy alloys synthesized as well-mixed, single-phase solid solutions with minimal compositional segregation.
generation.intervention: Subject samples to rapid, high-sensitivity differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) in an inert atmosphere while concurrently performing in-situ neutron imaging during controlled heating, followed by thermodynamic analysis via CALPHAD.
generation.conditions: Experiments conducted under inert gas to avoid oxidation, with carefully calibrated heating rates that traverse from below to above the melting point; measurements are taken for alloys that have uniform microstructures to minimize phase separation effects.
generation.structural_mediator: The high configurational entropy intrinsic to the alloy ensures atomic-scale homogeneity in the liquid state, facilitating reproducible thermal transitions and volume changes at melting.
generation.mechanism: DSC precisely identifies the endothermic peak associated with melting while neutron imaging captures real-time volumetric changes during fusion. CALPHAD modeling then refines these raw measurements into quantitative thermodynamic parameters by coupling the latent heat and volume expansion data with predictive thermodynamic databases.
generation.predicted_outcome: Fusion temperatures and latent heats can be determined within a 5–10% error relative to benchmarks from simpler alloys, with neutron imaging providing direct observation of the volume change at melting. Together, the integrated approach is expected to yield reliable, composition-dependent thermodynamic data across a broad range of high-entropy alloy systems.
generation.baseline: Traditional DSC measurements on less complex, simpler alloy systems that rely on slower heating rates and separate post-melting thermodynamic modeling.
generation.boundary: The approach is applicable primarily to high-entropy alloys that remain compositionally homogeneous at high temperatures; systems exhibiting significant liquid phase immiscibility or segregation may induce larger uncertainties.
generation.uncertainty: While the method is anticipated to deliver fusion property measurements within 5–10% accuracy, uncertainties may grow in alloys with extreme phase competition or when subtle ordering effects alter liquid state behavior.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of high-entropy alloy samples with varying but controlled compositions and microstructures. Then, perform simultaneous high-throughput DSC measurements and in-situ neutron imaging during controlled heating cycles. Independently calculate thermodynamic parameters using CALPHAD. Compare the measured melting temperatures, fusion enthalpies, fusion entropies, and volume changes with those predicted by CALPHAD and traditional methods over multiple repeated trials.
measurements: DSC endothermic peak integration for latent heat
Neutron imaging quantification of liquid-phase volume changes
Error analysis comparing integrated measurements with established benchmarks
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the integrated approach yields melting temperature, enthalpy, entropy, or volume change measurements that deviate by more than 10% from both established benchmark datasets and independent CALPHAD predictions, or if the real-time imaging fails to reliably correspond to DSC events, then the proposed method should be considered invalid.

High-Entropy Thermistor Ceramics (La1/3Nd1/3M1/3)2(Zr1/2Sn1/2)2O7 (M = Sm, Eu, Gd, or Dy) with High Sensitivity for High-Temperature Measurements

Abstract: AbstractA series of high-entropy pyrochlore ceramics, specifically (La1/3Nd1/3M1/3)2(Zn1/2Sn1/2)2O7 (M = Sm, Eu, Gd, or Dy), have been synthesized using the solid-state reaction method. Their potential as high-temperature thermistors was investigated by analyzing electrical and aging properties at elevated temperatures. Characterization using X-ray diffraction, scanning electron microscopy, and Raman spectroscopy confirms that these ceramics are dense, single-phase solid solutions with a pyrochlore structure. Electrical analysis demonstrate that these ceramics maintain high resistivity and resistance stability, exhibiting typical negative temperature coefficient features and high B values across a wide temperature range. Predictive multiphase evolution in Al-containing high-entropy alloys

Abstract: AbstractThe ability to predict and understand phases in high-entropy alloys (HEAs) is still being debated, and primarily true predictive capabilities derive from the known thermodynamics of materials. The present work demonstrates that prior work using high-throughput first-principles calculations may be further utilized to provide direct insight into the temperature- and composition-dependent phase evolution in HEAs, particularly Al-containing HEAs with a strengthening multiphase microstructure. Using a simple model with parameters derived from first-principles calculations, we reproduce the major features associated with Al-containing phases, demonstrating a generalizable approach for exploring potential phase evolution where little experimental data exists. Neutron scattering, in situ microscopy, and calorimetry measurements suggest that our high-throughput Monte Carlo technique captures both qualitative and quantitative features for both intermetallic phase formation and microstructure evolution at lower temperatures. In-Situ Imaging of Molten High-Entropy Alloys Using Cold Neutrons

Abstract: AbstractReal-time neutron imaging was utilized to produce a movie-like series of radiographs for in-situ observation of the remixing of liquid state immiscibility that occurs in equiatomic CoCrCu with the addition of Ni. A previous neutron imaging study demonstrated that liquid state immiscibility can be observed in-situ for the equiatomic CoCrCu alloy. In this follow-up study, equiatomic buttons of CoCrCu were placed alongside small Ni buttons inside an alumina crucible in a high-temperature vacuum furnace. The mass of the Ni buttons was specifically selected such that when melted in the same crucible as the CoCrCu buttons, the overall composition would become equiatomic CoCrCuNi. Neutron imaging was simultaneously carried out to capture 10 radiographs in 20 °C steps from 1000 °C to 1500 °C and back down to 1000 °C. This, in turn, produced a movie-like series of radiographs that allow for the observation of the buttons melting, the transition from immiscible to miscible as Ni is alloyed into the CoCrCu system, and solidification. Synthesis of Refractory High-Entropy Alloy WTaMoNbV by Powder Bed Fusion Process Using Mixed Elemental Alloying Powder

Abstract: AbstractThe growing interest in refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) in the last decade is mainly due to their thermal stability, outstanding mechanical properties, and excellent corrosion resistance. However, currently HEAs are still not considered for use as common structural materials due to their inherent drawbacks in terms of processing and machining operations. The recent progress witnessed in additive manufacturing (AM) technologies has raised the option of producing complex components made of HEAs with minimal machining processes. So far, this could be achieved by using pre-alloyed powders of HEAs that were mainly produced by a conventional arc melting furnace (AMF) in the form of small compounds that were transformed into powder via a gas atomization process. To significantly reduce the production cost, the present study aims to analyze the ability to synthesize HEA WTaMoNbV via a laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) process using mixed elemental alloying powder as the raw material.
